 Old favorites meet new UV technology, including BEMT, in the brand's ever-growing lineup. By Christa Joanna Lee November 12, 2026 Collage: Jemeria Davison; Source images: Courtesy of brands Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story We've all tried sunscreens that left us looking ghostly, feeling greasy, or blinking through watery eyes. The best La Roche-Posay sunscreens, thankfully, give us plenty of reasons to stick to wearing SPF daily. The French pharmacy favorite has built a solid reputation for its sun-protection formulas, with everything from lightweight serums to mineral options for sensitive skin and body lotions for seamless, all-over protection. They're all fragrance-free, too, which is one less thing for easily irritated skin to worry about.
 La Roche-Posay was also among the first to introduce a sunscreen with bemotrizinol (also known as BEMT ), a UV filter newly approved for use in the US. And with 25(!) sunscreens to choose from, there's a lot to sort through. Rather than leave you to play SPF roulette, we asked dermatologists for their picks and extensively tested the formulas ourselves to narrow down the field.

 Tasha Nicole Smith Allure commerce editor Sarah Han applying the La Roche-Posay Anthelios UVDefense SPF 50 Sunscreen with BEMT
 Sarah Han Why it's worth it: Some sunscreens win us over with their texture, others with their ingredients. La Roche-Posay's Anthelios UVDefense SPF 50 Sunscreen doesn't make us choose. It's among the first sunscreens to contain 2% bemotrizinol (BEMT), a newly FDA-approved sunscreen filter—and a pretty big deal, considering it's been more than two decades since the U.S. last approved a new one. BEMT protects against both UVA and UVB rays and is photostable, meaning it doesn't break down in sunlight. The formula also includes antioxidants that protect against skin-damaging free radicals, while glycerin , butylene glycol, and dimethicone moisturize skin and leave it feeling smooth.
 As for how it feels on your skin? "It's silky on the skin with no white residue," Jane Yoo , MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in New York City, previously told Allure . Even those with sensitive skin may get along with this formula, despite BEMT being a chemical sunscreen filter. "BEMT is a partial exception for those with sensitive skin because it is a huge molecule and it sits on the skin so there is minimal absorption," says Dr. Yoo.
 Tester feedback from commerce writer Tasha Nicole Smith 
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron “It’s been a long time since I’ve switched up my sunscreens, but this one proved to be well worth it. The formula was hydrating but didn’t feel at all heavy on my skin. The texture was lightweight and a bit silkier than I’m used to, which gave me pause at first, but it actually ended up being quite hydrating. Even when I reapplied throughout the day, I noticed a subtle glow on my skin, which is perfect because I love products that keep my dry skin looking glazed. It also didn’t sting or burn around my sensitive eyes. Definitely an SPF I’m excited to add to my rotation.” —Tasha Nicole Smith, commerce writer 
 Tester feedback from commerce editor Sarah Han 
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron "La Roche-Posay does it again. I love sunscreens that are on the more fluid side—think serum-like textures—and the Anthelios UVDefense SPF 50 Sunscreen with BEMT clearly falls under that umbrella! Like everyone in the beauty world, I'm ecstatic about a new UV filter, but I'm also hoping * taps watch * that the next approval doesn't take another 36 years. (We need to keep up with our global counterparts who are light-years ahead!!)
 Anyway, back to this formula. It's so lightweight and elegant that it practically disappears on contact, especially when you're applying two finger lengths' worth (the standard guideline). I was a little extra for this particular demo and used three fingers, so it did take a beat longer to fully rub in. Either way, the formula feels like nothing on the skin—and outside of the depths of winter—my combo skin and I don't need a standalone moisturizer because this doubles as both! The finish is definitely not as glowy as the UVAir serum , but these days, I kind of prefer a more ‘natural’ and ‘balanced’ look." —Sarah Han, commerce editor 
 How it compares to other La Roche-Posay sunscreens 
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The biggest difference here is the addition of BEMT, a UV filter you won't find in the other sunscreens on our list. Texture-wise, it's most similar to the UVAir Serum Sunscreen—which is a more fluid formula more akin to a serum than a traditional cream—though our testers found UVDefense has a more natural, less dewy finish.

 Shanna Shipin Why it's worth it: Do you like the idea of La Roche-Posay's Anthelios UVAir SPF 50 Serum Sunscreen but your skin tends to get along better with mineral formulas ? You’re in luck: This version swaps the chemical filters for 15.3% zinc oxide and 2.7% titanium dioxide, which may be a better match for sensitive skin that's easily irritated by chemical sunscreens. Of course, anyone who's tried mineral sunscreen knows it can be a challenge to avoid being left with a chalky white cast. La Roche-Posay addresses this with its Miner•ALL technology, which combines mineral filters with emollients like dimethicone that aid in spreading it more easily and feel lighter on your skin.
 Despite the different filters, the two formulas share plenty in common in terms of skin-care benefits. Both contain niacinamide to help even out skin tone, along with glycerin and hyaluronic acid to draw moisture into the skin without adding heaviness. They also share Senna alata leaf extract—a plant native to Central and South America widely used in traditional medicine—which contains antioxidants that help defend against free-radical damage that can contribute to premature signs of aging.
 Tester feedback from senior commerce director Shanna Shipin 
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron “I've heard many derms say, ‘The best sunscreen is the one you'll use every day,’ which makes UVAir the best for me! I have almost no qualms with this product—and that's saying a lot as someone who hasn't had quite a Goldilocks experience with mineral formulations. They're often thick, grainy, and leave a white cast. Not so with UV Air Mineral; as the name suggests, it's light as you-know-what, feels more like a serum than a sunscreen, and it instantly melts into the skin, disappearing in less than five seconds. This is one reason I use it more than any other mineral sunscreen; typically, you have to rub the formula in for at least 30 seconds for it to dissipate.
 As someone who's chronically late and has two kids, I really value beauty products that I don't need to wait on. The formula is very much like a serum, and that's the only slight negative; it's quite runny, so if you're not careful, you may drip some onto your clothes (or, in my case, the car, where I'm often reapplying). That said, it's far more stable than other formulas I've tried, so it's a small gripe (I hardly even have to shake it up before applying—another win!). The sunscreen is virtually undetectable on my medium skin tone, and I've never had any issues layering my typical makeup over top. It's also an adorable package; the sunscreen is stout, easy to squeeze out, and has a large top that feels intentional and sturdy when you close it. The formula uses chemical filters to shield skin from UVA and UVB rays, along with the brand's Cell-Ox B3 Shield technology, which adds another layer of defense with niacinamide (vitamin B3) and antioxidants like Senna alata leaf extract. Even with sunscreen on, UV exposure can generate free radicals—unstable molecules that contribute to fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots over time—and these antioxidants help neutralize them. And because nobody wants their sunscreen to dry out their skin, glycerin and hyaluronic acid hold onto moisture without weighing down the formula.
 And while the easily spreadable texture might tempt you to use less, don't hold back. You'll still want to apply about two finger lengths for adequate coverage.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Do higher concentrations of UV filters equate to better UV protection? 
 No, a higher percentage of any individual sunscreen filter—such as the buzzy, newly-approved BEMT—doesn't automatically mean better protection. “Protection comes from the whole formula, not from any single filter on the label,” says Dr. Yoo. “Also remember that SPF only measures UVB protection, the rays behind sunburn. UVA protection, which drives much of skin aging and pigment, is what the ‘broad spectrum’ claim tells you, and both come from testing the finished product.”
 Another factor to consider: Chemical UV filters are almost always one of multiple actives—yet more reasoning to look at each formula holistically. “BEMT, for example, covers both UVB and UVA, but it also helps keep other filters like avobenzone from breaking down in sunlight,” Dr. Yoo explains. “So a formula with 2% BEMT and a well-matched set of other filters can protect as well as one with 6% BEMT and a weaker supporting cast.” (Important context: The FDA only allows a maximum BEMT concentration of 6% in the US, while Europe allows up to 10%.)
 While we're discussing percentages, Kelly Dobos , a Cincinnati-based cosmetic chemist, had this to say about BEMT: “Unlike older filters that often require high concentrations to achieve adequate SPF, BEMT allows chemists to use lower overall levels of actives while still meeting high SPF and UVA protection targets." Therefore, comparing BEMT against other UV filters across different products/formulas is basically a moot point.
 So, what really matters when it comes to effective UV protection? “What tells you more is the SPF number, the words ‘broad spectrum,’ water resistance if you're sweating or swimming, and whether you like the texture enough to apply a generous layer and reapply every two hours .” As any dermatologist, beauty editor, or well-informed friend will tell you, the best sunscreen is one you'll actually use every day.

 How our staff tests and reviews products 
 When Allure tests a product , our editors look at it from every angle to best serve you. We review ingredients, scrutinize brand claims, and, when necessary, examine peer-reviewed scientific and medical studies. In addition to testing each and every product that's included in each and every review, we rely on experts who shape their fields, including dermatology, cosmetic chemistry, and medicine, to help us vet the ingredients and formulas.
 For our list of the best La Roche-Posay sunscreens, we considered each product's performance across five primary categories: product ingredients and efficacy, packaging, fragrance, texture, and product wear. Every product was determined to have excelled in each category by our editorial team, which is composed of in-house writers and editors as well as contributors—along with special consideration from board-certified dermatologists. To learn more information on our reporting and testing processes, read our complete reviews process and methodology page .
 Meet our staff and testers 
 A beauty product is a personal purchase. You might be searching for a face cream to address persistent dryness or a new nail product to add to your Sunday self-care routine; you may simply be browsing around for the latest launches to hit the hair market. No matter what you seek or your individual needs and concerns, Allure wants to ensure that you love anything we recommend in our stories. We believe that having a diverse team of writers and editors — in addition to the wide range of outside testers and industry experts we regularly call upon — is essential to reaching that goal.
 After all, can we really say a skin-care product is the "best" for people over 50 if the only testers we've solicited opinions from folks who have yet to hit 30? Can we honestly deem a high-end diffuser worthy of your hard-earned cash if it’s never been tested on curls? We're proud that our staff spans a wide range of ages, skin tones, hair textures, genders, and backgrounds, which means that we are able to fairly assess any beauty product that comes into the beauty closet.
